title: E23 - Investment Hype vs. Reality in Legal AI, Eli Amsellem, Ridge Ventures
author: Eli Amsellem

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source addresses legal AI’s commercial value, buyer demand, adoption and investment risk, not whether automating junior work undermines expertise reproduction or how apprenticeship should be reconstructed. Its suggestion that expertise may move in-house and reduce external-law-firm spending is only tangentially relevant and does not establish a position on associate training.
qs: You know, is there a reason to be spending so much, not just in terms of, hey, reducing headcount, but like what kind of expertise can be democratized and bring in house and save dollars allocating that to outsource legal firms or whatever it may be.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts Harvey’s traction and product strength while materially extending the cluster’s durability question into venture economics: strong adoption and capable teams may still lack defensibility and long-term venture-scale returns. It also identifies productized expertise distributed to in-house buyers as a possible route to scale.
qs: So at the application layer, listen, I think in venture you always have to understand just because you have a great product doesn't mean you have a great business.
But the game itself is so competitive that you wonder, can there really be, you know, the kind of long term VC returns?

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s buyer-led transformation thesis, arguing that legal expertise can be productized for in-house use and reduce reliance on outside counsel. It materially extends the synthesis with an investment and distribution lens: durable value depends on retention, defensible specialist markets, embedded data and cross-market sales, while early adoption and automation expectations remain uncertain. It does not substantially address pricing or apprenticeship.
qs: The question is, hey, can you build a tool you need to, working with those high-end lawyers, understanding how they work, understanding the expertise they have, productizing it, and then you democratize that intelligence you captured to in-house.
I think people are moving too quickly a bit in terms of their expectations.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Amsellem accepts that AI can transfer legal expertise into corporate legal departments and reduce selected outside-counsel spending. He materially extends the cluster by arguing that durable in-house adoption, customer-embedded development and accumulated institutional data—not initial contracts or compelling demos—determine whether this shift creates defensible vendor value.
qs: You know, is there a reason to be spending so much, not just in terms of, hey, reducing headcount, but like what kind of expertise can be democratized and bring in house and save dollars allocating that to outsource legal firms or whatever it may be.
So we like to see that actually across all segments, like really sitting side by side, building early product and being deployed with, you know, ensuring adoption, I like to say.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI can address document-intensive legal work and that value may depend on specialised workflows and embedded legal context. It materially extends the synthesis by distinguishing buyer needs and budgets, framing value beyond headcount reduction, and adding investment and valuation-risk considerations, while leaving horizontal assistance versus vertical workflow automation unresolved.
qs: AI in terms of specifically summarizing and then also generating content, whether it be long legal documents where literally no old lawyers are doing, and everyone in this legal office is just going through, trying to understand the nuances here, sometimes having to play towards a playbook that they've been handed off on their desk from 15 years of a firm's expertise and practices and risk tolerance.

Plus, we go deep on a couple of companies like Harvey, Legora, NewCode, OpenPolicy, and Legalmation, and we debate whether the future is in horizontal AI assistance or vertical workflow automation that no one sees coming.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s hybrid, buyer-driven model and materially extends it with an investor lens: legal-AI providers must productise lawyer expertise for in-house teams while building durable value through client-specific data, retention and defensibility. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that early contracts and adoption do not yet prove scalable transformation.
qs: The question is, hey, can you build a tool you need to, working with those high-end lawyers, understanding how they work, understanding the expertise they have, productizing it, and then you democratize that intelligence you captured to in-house.

But hey, is there like underlying data that they're capturing and organizing for this law firm, where there's like kind of compounding value being built as data is getting poured in there, as they're learning how to utilize it, as they quickly extract terms from deals or extract details from particular larger cases.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Amsellem accepts that current AI requires human involvement and that expectations are outrunning capability, while materially extending the cluster’s operating-model argument: durable value should come from deeply integrated, customer-specific workflow automation rather than lightly embedded assistants. His claims are primarily investor judgment and anecdote, not controlled evidence, but they concretely develop the redesign thesis.
qs: Are they deeply embedded in their workflows and have all the integrations they need?
And okay, we're going to go AI first, but our version of AI first is now with humans in the loop, and we have to actually bring everyone back to office.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source broadly supports the proposition that legal AI’s value depends on applying language-model capabilities to expertise-intensive, document-heavy work and adapting tools to buyer-specific needs, playbooks and risk tolerances. It does not materially address agentic workflow design, expert testing, human checkpoints or the difficulty of transferring tacit expertise, so its support is narrower than the cluster synthesis.
qs: AI in terms of specifically summarizing and then also generating content, whether it be long legal documents where literally no old lawyers are doing, and everyone in this legal office is just going through, trying to understand the nuances here, sometimes having to play towards a playbook that they've been handed off on their desk from 15 years of a firm's expertise and practices and risk tolerance.
They talk about what tools they use, they talk about their pain points, and it's a great ground for understanding, hey, what are they actually looking to buy?

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s conditional optimism: it distinguishes skepticism from blanket rejection and remains enthusiastic about legal-tech companies. It offers no evidence or substantive extension concerning user-led adoption, verification, autonomy, or market outcomes.
qs: And yeah, I know I might sound really skeptical, but I am excited about a lot of legal tech companies and chat and try to provide as much help as possible.
So don't think that I've already written you off, face off things I've said.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: Amsellem supports the synthesis’s cautious, unresolved framing: he treats legal AI as practically compelling while using the prior CLM valuation boom to show that product utility and investment enthusiasm do not establish durable vendor economics or determine which application-layer model will prevail. He does not address the competing infrastructure architectures in detail.
qs: I would say what's shocking, if you think about all the money that's pouring in right now, is that in 20 through 22, you had the sort of CLM craze, and everyone investing money in companies and giving them these unicorn, you know, excess billion-dollar valuations.
But I think one of the big questions is like the AI application layer, right?

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis by treating Harvey’s elite law-firm partnerships as a possible distribution route into corporate legal departments while distinguishing strong traction from durable application-layer defensibility or venture-scale success. Its interpretation is explicitly outside-in and speculative, reinforcing the synthesis’s evidentiary cautions rather than proving accuracy, productivity or lasting differentiation.
qs: What we want to do is through our partnerships with those law firms, sell to their clients and sort of embed ourselves in a whole chunk of the industry.

Like Harvey is showing wild, wild numbers, and yet there is definitely a feeling, maybe it's a little bit FOMO induced, but I think there is a feeling amongst some investors that ChatGPT for lawyers, which is effectively what Harvey and Legora and others like it are, may not necessarily be like the best move long-term, although it's got Sequoia and Kleiner-Perkins and others behind it.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that practical AI usefulness and initial adoption do not by themselves create durable commercial advantage. It emphasizes that law-firm contracts may be provisional and that lasting value depends on whether applications capture, organize and compound firm data, while narrowing its analysis mainly to vendor retention and investment risk rather than pricing, staffing or buyer power.
qs: And they'll say, yeah, like, listen, we're happy to try this tool for a year.

But hey, is there like underlying data that they're capturing and organizing for this law firm, where there's like kind of compounding value being built as data is getting poured in there, as they're learning how to utilize it, as they quickly extract terms from deals or extract details from particular larger cases.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster by treating AI value as contingent on buyer-specific needs, purchasing behaviour and budgets rather than technical capability alone. It also supports the cluster’s qualified scenarios around premium pricing, insourcing and reduced outside-counsel spend, while presenting these as commercial possibilities rather than demonstrated sector-wide effects.
qs: They talk about what tools they use, they talk about their pain points, and it's a great ground for understanding, hey, what are they actually looking to buy?

You know, is there a reason to be spending so much, not just in terms of, hey, reducing headcount, but like what kind of expertise can be democratized and bring in house and save dollars allocating that to outsource legal firms or whatever it may be.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that funding and adoption signals do not establish durable vendor value. It distinguishes headline valuations and apparent recurring revenue from retention and venture suitability, while identifying foundation-model competition and leaving horizontal versus vertical strategies unresolved. Its claims are introductory and anecdotal rather than systematic evidence.
qs: You've got customers that aren't really customers, revenue that's technically recurring, but only until next year's innovation budget disappears, and the constant looming threat of getting steamrolled by open AI.

We talk about why so much adoption is actually smoke and mirrors, how big law is treating legal AI like a one-year trial marriage, why some of the best-looking start-ups might still be bad VC bets, and what it really takes to build something sticky in this space.

kp.k: Buyer interviews underpin Amsellem's investment thesis
kp.d: Amsellem describes Ridge's research as conversations with law-firm partners, GCs and 60, 70 plus companies, supplemented by recurring GC dinners. These provide qualitative buyer intelligence, not a systematic adoption study. He stresses differences between law firms and in-house teams in pain points, purchasing patterns and available budgets.
qs: I chatted with 60, 70 plus companies looking for something interesting, and looking for one of those sub segments within legal.
We actually host multiple GC dinners throughout the year.
Are the buying patterns the same? Are the dollars behind them that they can allocate budget towards the same? Not always

kp.k: Generative AI could internalize outsourced legal expertise
kp.d: Amsellem argues that legal work is particularly suited to generative AI because it combines extensive reading and drafting with specialized interpretation and accumulated institutional playbooks. He frames the opportunity as efficiency and bringing expertise in-house to reduce external legal spending, rather than merely reducing headcount; these are proposed mechanisms rather than measured outcomes.
qs: not just in terms of, hey, reducing headcount, but like what kind of expertise can be democratized and bring in house and save dollars allocating that to outsource legal firms

specifically within legal where it is manual hours of a lot of content being ingested, a lot of content being poured out, and then also having to have an expertise where you know what to look for, understand the nuances within this content.

kp.k: Good legal products need not deliver venture returns
kp.d: Amsellem distinguishes product quality, business viability and venture-scale returns. He expects many legal-AI businesses to produce worthwhile founder outcomes without delivering the 20, 50, 100X returns sought by venture investors, and predicts that many currently funded companies will disappoint expectations. Abramowitz separately invokes the 20 through 22 CLM investment boom as a caution about valuations exceeding plausible exit values.
qs: just because you have a great product doesn't mean you have a great business. Just because you have a great business doesn't mean you have a great venture backable business.
the scope of where we could really put in dollars with a lot of confidence that you can actually get that 20, 50, 100X back to your LPs is a lot smaller than people think
in 20 through 22, you had the sort of CLM craze
some of them today have sort of raised beyond a valuation that they could probably go public at.

kp.k: Niche market creation differs from constrained task markets
kp.d: Amsellem presents Ridge portfolio company OpenPolicy as a favorable niche: AI identifies company-relevant public regulatory material and supports comments, communications and participation in policy coalitions, potentially broadening capabilities previously reserved for large companies. By contrast, he sees patent research as a useful AI application whose customer base, willingness to pay and obtainable value may limit venture outcomes. These are investment judgments, including a disclosed portfolio interest.
qs: OpenPolicy, which is a company we invested in

OpenPolicy is democratizing that, it's essentially using AI to capture all that data, distill it into specifically what's relevant for a company, giving them opportunity through AI to actually write comments, participate in consortiums and coalitions.
There is a lot of value in essentially creating a market.
But the amount of dollars you command there, the amount of value you can drive, I think it's limited in terms of who you could sell this to, who actually needs it, how much they're willing to pay.

kp.k: In-house expansion could unlock larger vendor outcomes
kp.d: Amsellem argues that large law firms can support initial $1-2 million software contracts but offer limited loyalty. His proposed route to venture-scale returns is to productize expertise learned from high-end lawyers and sell it to in-house teams. He also identifies broad mid-market and small-firm segments, such as personal injury, as possible alternatives, while warning that competition and weak defensibility remain obstacles.
qs: They don't mind paying $1-2 million for a software tool.
But they also are not married to anything. They're not loyal to any tools.
understanding the expertise they have, productizing it, and then you democratize that intelligence you captured to in-house. That's where I think the VC outcome is possible.
I just think in that space, it's really just a dogfight because the tooling you're going to build is not necessarily almost defensible.

kp.k: Embedded engineering becomes a desirable investment signal
kp.d: Amsellem says venture investors previously treated engineers working inside customer offices as an unattractive services component, whereas Ridge now favors this approach for comprehensive enterprise AI. He regards close customer collaboration, integrations and workflow-specific development as signals of adoption and retention potential rather than proof of durable revenue.
qs: with every single client we sell to, we're wrapping up three or four engineers were sitting in their offices

We want to see, are these founders or the early engineering team sitting side by side with these customers? Are they building products specifically catered to their needs? Are they deeply embedded in their workflows and have all the integrations they need?
Are they building something that's going to be super sticky? Are they actually solving problems that these customers have?

kp.k: Accumulated knowledge may create stronger switching barriers
kp.d: Amsellem predicts that Harvey's Vault knowledge-base module, rather than interface design or drafting and summarization quality, could sustain its position inside firms. His proposed retention mechanism is compounding value from organizing firm data and extracting deal terms and case details. This is a forecast about product defensibility, not documented retention performance.
qs: they built the Vault Module, which is essentially like their knowledge base, where I think will ultimately be the reason they stay embedded in a lot of the law firms
is there like underlying data that they're capturing and organizing for this law firm, where there's like kind of compounding value being built as data is getting poured in there

kp.k: Annual contracts can conceal experimental purchasing
kp.d: Drawing on conversations with partners and innovation groups, Amsellem reports that firms can treat annual contracts, sometimes 100k plus, as proofs of concept and reconsider vendors after a year. Abramowitz corroborates the concern through his own reported knowledge of firms buying two products and a secondhand account of annual pilot budgets of one to two million dollars. Neither provides measured renewal or churn rates.
qs: annual contracts with these law firms, usually like pretty big ACVs, maybe like 100k plus
We talk to these law firms directly, talk to the partners and these innovation groups.
we're happy to try this tool for a year. Right now, this is what's in market.
But ultimately for them, that first year contract is a POC, and they're happy to jump over.
And to the outside eye, it all looks like recurring revenue. But it might not be.

kp.k: Innovation signaling can drive unstable vendor choices
kp.d: Abramowitz suggests early Harvey relationships helped firms signal innovation to clients and employees, but that this differentiation diminishes as adoption spreads. He interprets Harvey's partnerships as a possible channel into law-firm clients, explicitly acknowledging this as an outside interpretation rather than inside knowledge. He argues that innovation officers' reputational objectives could favor different tools in 2025 and 2027.
qs: a number of the first firms that went with Harvey could sort of claim to be innovative and look innovative by dint of their relationship with Harvey
I'm saying this not with knowing it from people in Harvey, sort of looking from the outside in.
What we want to do is through our partnerships with those law firms, sell to their clients and sort of embed ourselves in a whole chunk of the industry.
So what make you look innovative in 2025 might be something other than 2027.

kp.k: Workflow automation may outlast faster-growing AI assistants
kp.d: Abramowitz relays another podcast guest's prediction that automating complete workflows, especially outsourced work or work handled by a retiring workforce, will generate stickier revenue than general AI assistants. He endorses this distinction through Legalmation, disclosing his investment and saying that the company launched in 2019 and has grown more slowly than Harvey but handles a more durable workflow. His claim of permanent retention is an investor assertion, not supported here by customer data.
qs: what will be stickier over time to businesses is where you are able to automate an entire workflow
his point was that's going to be the stickier revenue, even if it's not the fast growing revenue that you're talking about today.
I'm an investor in Legalmation. Legalmation has not grown nearly as fast as Harvey and was launched, you know, in 2019.
But the workflow they handle is a much, much stickier workflow.

kp.k: Diligence should distinguish software budgets from experimentation
kp.d: Amsellem recommends asking whether spending comes from innovation budgets or replaces existing software. He cautions that executive enthusiasm and generic efficiency metrics may coexist with limited internal use and that serious errors could undermine adoption after a year or two. His hypothetical $100 million case-loss example is not identified as a documented legal incident. He also uses an imprecisely described customer-support automation reversal as a cross-industry warning about premature expectations and the need for humans in the loop.
qs: a particular question we'll always ask is where is the budget coming from, whether it's coming from the innovation budget versus like, hey, this is actual our actual software spend.
are you replacing another tool with this AI first tool or are you just testing it out?
you'll ask for like metrics and they'll have like some high level generic metrics that really mean nothing.
our version of AI first is now with humans in the loop
I think people are moving too quickly a bit in terms of their expectations.

kp.k: Competitive imitation could concentrate law-firm software adoption
kp.d: Amsellem argues that large firms' competitive imitation creates opportunities for a best-in-class vendor to achieve unusually broad penetration. He cites iManage's claimed 80% distribution within the AmLaw 200 as an analogy and predicts that widespread use among leading firms could make procurement and willingness to pay increasingly compulsory for competitors. The transcript supplies no independent substantiation for the market-share figure.
qs: They have 80% distribution within Amlog 200.
It'll be, I know every single one of the Amlog 10 firms uses this particular tool. It's best in class and I need to use it too.
We're going to pay whatever they tell us to pay because we need to compete.

kp.k: Efficiency pressures challenge pricing without immediate model replacement
kp.d: Amsellem describes client expectations for faster delivery, smaller teams, greater expertise and lower billable hours as pressures on firms' economics. He illustrates a possible response with partners charging 3K per hour while using AI, but questions where value will accrue. He rejects predictions that the entire charging model will be overturned and rebuilt within the next few years; the staffing and pricing examples are illustrative rather than measured outcomes.
qs: the billables are expected to be lower. You're expected to have more expertise. They want you to move a lot quicker.
going to be less billable hours, but we're going to now charge you 3K per hour for these partners time.
So where does the dollar value come out? It's questionable.
everyone was just talking about that whole model falling on its head and then re-creating how they charge. It's unrealistic in the next few years.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Eli Amsellem predicts substantial legal-work efficiency gains but selective venture-scale opportunities, with durable adoption depending on workflow integration, accumulated data and expansion beyond large law firms.
pts.d: Amsellem (00:05:35) argues that generative AI is especially applicable to legal work because it involves extensive document ingestion, generation and contextual expertise. Its value includes bringing expertise in-house and reducing outside legal expenditure, not merely reducing headcount. At 00:10:18–00:13:59, he distinguishes useful products and successful businesses from venture-backable businesses, predicting that many funded legal-AI companies will not achieve investors' expected outcomes. He identifies opportunities in transferring expertise learned from large law firms to in-house teams, serving sufficiently large specialist markets such as personal injury, and creating niche markets such as OpenPolicy's AI-assisted regulatory and public-affairs work. He considers patent research useful but constrained by customer numbers and willingness to pay. At 00:20:03, he argues that engineers working alongside customers, workflow integrations and accumulated firm data support retention; he singles out Harvey's Vault knowledge base as a prospective source of durable embeddedness rather than interface or drafting quality alone. He also claims large firms often treat annual contracts as proofs of concept and can switch horizontal AI tools. At 00:27:56, he predicts that an eventual error or hallucination could reverse customer enthusiasm, while suggesting that early spending and deployment can help vendors build competitive products. At 00:29:55, he claims competitive imitation can spread a best-in-class tool across large firms. AI simultaneously raises client expectations of speed and expertise and puts pressure on billable hours, but he does not expect a wholesale reconstruction of charging models in the next few years.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily Amsellem's investor diligence, buyer conversations and product observations, rather than quantified outcome or retention studies.
pts.d: At 00:03:09 and 00:10:18, Amsellem describes research with more than 60–70 companies, conversations with law-firm partners and general counsel, and recurring GC dinners. His account of annual contracts functioning as trials draws on direct conversations with partners and innovation groups (00:20:03). His argument about Harvey's in-house expansion references changes to its website, while the Vault retention thesis is his prospective interpretation of the product's data-accumulation value, not a reported retention measurement. He discloses that Ridge invested in OpenPolicy. He criticises generic customer efficiency metrics but supplies no systematic alternative measurements. His scenario involving loss of a $100 million case is a possible future consequence, with no named case or measured hallucination rate supplied. He invokes iManage's claimed 80% penetration of the AmLaw 200 as an analogy for large-firm adoption concentration; no supporting dataset is identified. His venture-return, patent-market and billing-model assessments are investment judgments and predictions. Host claims about surveys and Legalmation, and the host's account of another person's workflow-automation thesis, are not treated here as Amsellem's evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the 2025 market, annual renewal decisions and longer-term defensibility; Amsellem explicitly anticipates possible problems after one or two years and rejects near-term wholesale billing reform.
pts.d: Amsellem's adoption and investment observations describe the market at the time of the 2025 interview. Large-firm willingness to buy does not, in his account, establish long-term loyalty: the first annual contract can be a trial, followed by reassessment against competing products. Whether expenditure comes from an innovation budget or replaces an existing software purchase is an important condition for interpreting adoption. Retention is conditional on deep workflow integration and accumulated data creating value that is harder to transfer. Venture-scale outcomes depend on sufficient market size and spend, including the ability to expand into in-house teams or reach a large specialist law-firm market; he does not set an exit date. At 00:27:56, he suggests failures might emerge after a year or two rather than within the first few months, and says expectations are moving too quickly. At 00:29:55, he qualifies the billing-disruption thesis: client pressure is already occurring, but a fundamental reconstruction of charging models is unrealistic over the next few years. His references to reduced staffing, tenfold delivery speed and higher partner rates are illustrative competitive scenarios, not measured universal effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include large firms and their lawyers, corporate legal buyers, specialist smaller firms, public-affairs teams, legal-AI vendors and venture investors.
pts.d: For large firms, Amsellem describes substantial software purchasing capacity, competitive pressure to adopt leading tools, and flexibility to change suppliers. Lawyers face expectations of faster work and greater expertise with fewer billable hours; partners might compensate through higher hourly rates, although the ultimate distribution of value remains uncertain. Corporate GCs and in-house teams are potential recipients of expertise productised from high-end law-firm work, allowing more work to be handled internally and less spending on outside firms. Mid-market and smaller specialist firms, particularly personal-injury practices, can collectively support substantial vendor businesses, although he sees weak tooling defensibility and intense competition. Corporate IP teams are potential patent-research customers, but their number and willingness to pay may limit vendor scale. OpenPolicy's target users are public- and government-affairs personnel at companies seeking regulatory intelligence and opportunities to comment or participate in coalitions; this is business capability expansion, not an access-to-justice claim. Vendors must distinguish initial sales from durable recurring demand, while founders and investors face different definitions of a successful outcome: a good business need not deliver venture-scale returns.
